activities.caption: walk the defence and the rebuttal
activities.name: stratDMBranch

config.root: Why do surgeons out-earn messengers? A 1945 defence, and the withering rebuttal:

choices.label: Society must reward scarce, important roles — or no one would train
The rich are simply better organised

mis1.text: Not the 1945 argument — theirs is an incentive claim about scarce, important roles.

dm2.text: Now the rebuttal: what does the reward system actually pay for?

choices.label: Access to training as much as for talent — reproducing the accessors' advantages

mis2.text: That is exactly what the rebuttal denies — payment tracks access as much as ability.

tum2.text: And the mispricing: care work and sanitation, functionally vital, sit at the bottom of the pay scale. So the level of inequality is…?

choices.label: A choice the 1945 logic cannot itself explain — functioning societies retain incentives with far less spread

mis3.text: Functioning societies clearly can retain incentive structures with far less spread — the level is a choice.

end.text: The defence explains some spread; it cannot explain how much.

config.why: Scarce roles deserve reward; but payment tracks access and misprices vital work — and the spread that remains is a choice.

activities.caption: find the faulty line — the compression record
activities.name: stratCompressionSpot

config.prompt: One line of this summary is wrong — click it:
lines: The Great Compression (US, 1940s–1970s): top income shares fell steeply, then re-concentrated from the 1980s.
Esping-Andersen's liberal regimes are means-tested and market-dominant — the US.
Social-democratic regimes — Sweden — are universal and decommodifying.
The Nordic evidence shows high equality costs growth — compression buys stagnation.
The low-inequality countries stack many levers rather than relying on one.
config.correction: High equality coexists with high growth in the Nordics — universal services plus progressive taxation compress the distribution before and after earnings.
config.why: No single lever does it — the low-gap countries stack many levers, and the mobility they buy comes mostly from removing price tags from childhood.

config.prompt: After 1978, how many people did China alone lift out of extreme poverty?
config.why: About 800 million — and the global extreme-poverty rate fell from roughly 38% in 1990 to under 10% by the late 2010s.
